population.note: FICTIONAL estimates. 17% of ~265M adults ≈ 45M current users, all indications (obesity, diabetes, 'metabolic/longevity'). Age check: 0.20×8 + 0.33×17 + 0.24×28 + 0.23×14 ≈ 17.2. Of the 45M, about 5.3M (≈2% of adults) have no obesity and use low-dose orals or injectables for 'metabolic health' or longevity. They pay cash and are concentrated in the top income third. Cycling arithmetic: ever 23 − current 17 = 6 pp of adults have used the drug and are off now. About 7 pp of the 17 on the drug are restarters, and about 1.5 pp of the 6 off-now restarted once and then stopped again, so (7 + 1.5) / 23 ≈ 37% of ever-users have cycled. This fits 1-year persistence of ~35–40% and 36–47% restart within a year, since survey 'ever' figures undercount short trial courses. The 6 pp off-now (~16M adults) are mainly people who stopped over cost or GI effects in 2026–27, people pushed off by the Oct 2027–Jun 2028 semaglutide shortage, and older users told to pause after fracture or sarcopenia findings. About a fifth of US adults with obesity have never been able to get the drug through any channel. The bottom third gained mainly through Medicaid opt-in states, partly offset by adult Medicaid work requirements in force from 2027. Pediatric: ~1.1% of under-18s are on the drug, almost all aged 12–17 on semaglutide or liraglutide (including generic liraglutide). Under-12 use is still specialist-only and still skews to upper-income families.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge pilot (Jul 2026–Dec 2027) was replaced in Jan 2028 by a CMS Innovation Center model running through 2031. The $245 Medicare payment and ~$50 copay are unchanged, the BMI/comorbidity criteria are slightly loosened, and Zepbound, Wegovy (injectable and oral), Foundayo and CagriSema are covered. Retatrutide is not yet included. About 9.0M Medicare enrollees are on an incretin, ~3.2M of them under the obesity model. Gross obesity-model spend: 3.2M × $245 × 12 ≈ $9.4B/yr. Medicaid: 31 states opted into obesity coverage at the same $245 rate. ~5.0M Medicaid users, ~2.2M of them for obesity. Obesity spend: 2.2M × $245 × 12 ≈ $6.5B/yr, of which ~65% federal ≈ $4.2B. VA, TRICARE and other public payers cover ~1.0M. Public payers total ~15M of 45M users (≈33%) and ~40% of new obesity starts in 2028, the largest single payer type for new starts and the default payer for anyone over 65.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 60+ brands, ~$6–40/month. Canada: several generics at ~CAD 70–110/month; Health Canada limits dispensing to non-residents, but US personal imports through border pharmacies (Windsor, Ontario; Vancouver) are tolerated under FDA personal-use discretion. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and much of Southeast Asia have generic semaglutide. Cost-plus generic injectable is available in ~170 countries.
access.note: List prices unchanged: Wegovy $1,349, Ozempic ~$998. The price and availability shock is in the cash channel. After Novo's Bloomington, Indiana fill-finish site halted in Oct 2027, cash semaglutide injectable went from $349 to $499. Lilly ended its lowest-tier Zepbound vial promotions, and higher-dose vials now cost $549–649. Novo rationed new oral Wegovy starts, because the 25 mg daily oral uses roughly 70× the API of a weekly 2.4 mg injection. The median monthly price paid by uninsured cash users rose from ~$350 (2026) to ~$470 (2028). Foundayo's lowest dose stayed at $149 via LillyDirect/TrumpRx, and Medicare and Medicaid prices stayed at $245, so the shock fell on cash payers and the commercially insured, not on public enrollees. Semaglutide was on the FDA shortage list from Oct 2027 to Jun 2028, which legally reopened 503A compounding. About 1.5M people used compounded product at the peak, and an estimated ~0.9M were still on compounded or imported product at end-2028 during the FDA wind-down. Payer mix of 45M users: public ~15M (33%), commercial ~16M (36%), cash/direct ~14M (31%, including ~5M non-obese 'metabolic' users). Employer coverage for weight management fell from 60% to 50% (fictional survey), and several large retailers and hospital systems cited Medicare as 'where obesity care now lives'.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Jan 2027)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Apr 2028)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: cardiovascular risk reduction (semaglutide 2024; tirzepatide 2027 on SURPASS-CVOT)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'Metabolic health' and longevity use by people without obesity (~2% of US adults), mostly low-dose oral via telehealth and longevity clinics, paid in cash

'Quiet mind' / 'food-noise-and-rumination' programmes: telehealth firms market low-dose GLP-1 for focus and calm through lifestyle claims, with no approved psychiatric indication; this is the commercial form of the mood_and_motivation driver
Alcohol reduction: Novo phase 3 of oral semaglutide in alcohol use disorder is enrolling; widely prescribed off-label for heavy drinkers with overweight
Pediatric under-12 use off-label under specialist care
Nicotine and other compulsion reduction: observational and anecdotal
drugs.pipeline_note: CagriSema was approved Jan 2027 after its late-2026 review. It is positioned as a 'tolerability' option, not an efficacy leader, because of its REDEFINE-4 result. Retatrutide's BLA was filed Mar 2027 and approved Apr 2028, 13 months later. The label covers dysesthesia, and new class language on lean mass and bone density applies to it. Launch list price is $1,299/month, it is excluded from the Medicare model pending negotiation, and commercial uptake is gated by prior authorisation. Amycretin is in phase 3 and not filed. Survodutide read out phase 3 in 2027, was filed in Q3 2028, and cannot be approved before late 2029. Monthly dosing (next_gen_launch driver): no monthly incretin or implant is on the US market. The approval rules allow only a filing in this window, so the driver is realised by Amgen filing the MariTide (maridebart cafraglutide) monthly-injection BLA in Nov 2028, with a decision no earlier than late 2029. Payers, CMS and employers are already modelling 'adherence by default' on that basis. Bimagrumab and other muscle-preserving adjuncts are in phase 2–3 and not on the market. Global incretin market estimated at ~$110B in 2028.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Shortage-forced switches between molecules in 2027–28 caused a wave of re-titration GI complaints, because many switchers restarted at too high a dose.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; Ozempic label 'not recommended in severe gastroparesis' unchanged. FDA switching guidance issued during the shortage.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss; more visible with retatrutide-scale losses.
No causal confirmation in long-term RCTs; absolute risk low.

Now a recognised population problem, no longer only a trial footnote. Real-world DXA cohorts in users 65+ with ≥15% weight loss show lean mass at ~35–40% of weight lost, worse than the 25–30% trial figure. Sarcopenia diagnosis codes among Medicare incretin users roughly doubled from 2026 to 2028, partly because of increased screening.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class labelling (Aug 2028) on lean mass loss and bone mineral density for all incretin obesity products. CMS model guidance recommends functional screening (grip strength, chair-rise) at 12 months for enrollees 65+ and covers resistance-training referral. Screening is recommended, not a condition of coverage.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture in older and long-term users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: NEW, part of the muscle_bone_wave. Pooled US Medicare claims and Danish registry analyses (Mar 2028) found hip fracture hazard ratio ~1.3 in users 65+ with rapid ≥15% loss in the first two years, and a smaller signal in users of any age on continuous therapy beyond 3 years. Baseline hip fracture risk is ~0.7%/yr in this group, so the excess is ~0.2 pp/yr, or roughly 6,000 additional hip fractures a year across ~3.2M Medicare obesity-model users. The effect is attenuated in users doing resistance training with adequate protein intake.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA Drug Safety Communication (Mar 2028) followed by class label update (Aug 2028). Endocrine and geriatric societies advise slower titration and target loss caps for adults over 70. No coverage restriction.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Further cohorts still conflict; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label stands; no US class label.
Warning removed from US labels (2026); unchanged.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Moved from emerging to suspected. In a fictional 2028 national survey, ~27% of current users report feeling 'flat' or 'less like myself' at some point and ~20% have skipped or reduced doses to restore it. There is still no RCT designed to measure it, and one small 2027 crossover study found modest dose-dependent drops in self-reported reward responsiveness.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. FDA has asked sponsors for anhedonia-scale data in ongoing trials, and NIH funded a cohort study. Telehealth firms sell the same effect as 'quiet mind'.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Real-world regain is substantial but smaller than in STEP-1. The forced interruptions of the 2027–28 shortage gave a natural experiment: median regain was ~40% of lost weight within 8 months among those who could not switch.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; reinforces the chronic-therapy framing and the payer interest in monthly dosing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Overlaps with the protein and bone findings; low protein intake is a common factor.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Nutrition counselling recommended in CMS model guidance; no label.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exist. The bone findings are the first long-horizon signal to firm up. No adolescent bone-accrual data yet, which is a growing concern for 12–17 users during peak bone-mass years.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on new approvals (Foundayo, CagriSema, retatrutide), including adolescent bone-density substudies.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Resurged during the Oct 2027–Jun 2028 shortage-list window, when 503A compounding became legal again. FDA adverse-event reports tied to compounded product passed ~3,000. Counterfeit pens seized in personal imports.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B bulks-list exclusion finalised (Feb 2027). Wind-down period for 503A compounding after the shortage was declared resolved in Jun 2028. Warning letters continue.

food_and_beverage.state: Incretin households are ~30% of US households (fictional). Snack and confectionery volumes are down an estimated 3–5% cumulatively since 2026, while revenue is held up by price and pack architecture. Protein, fibre and 'bone and muscle' callouts, such as calcium plus protein, replaced 'GLP-1-friendly' as the dominant claim after the fracture news. The shortage months gave a brief, measurable bump in snack volume in affected regions, a data point CPG analysts now quote.

alcohol.state: US spirits and beer volumes keep falling, with the heaviest-drinking decile shrinking fastest. Brown-Forman and Diageo cut US sales forces and pushed RTD, low-ABV and non-alcoholic lines, which grow but do not replace lost margin. The 'one good drink' premium occasion is the surviving segment.

restaurants.state: Traffic roughly flat, with average check per diner down slightly in casual dining. Small-plates and 'half-portion' menus are standard at Darden and similar chains. Fine dining sells tasting menus as 'occasion eating'. Buffet formats keep closing.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep closing stores, and Torrid and DXL shrink footprints further. Mainstream brands benefit from re-sizing churn. Shortage-driven regain produced a minor rebound in 'in-between' sizing and stretch fabrics.

fitness.state: Growing. Strength training is the product, and after the Mar 2028 fracture communication gyms market 'bone and muscle insurance'. Medicare Advantage fitness benefits (SilverSneakers-type) see their highest enrollment in resistance classes. Physical-therapy chains run 'GLP-1 strength' programmes billed through the CMS referral pathway.

insurance.state: Employer coverage for weight management is down to ~50%, with those dropping it citing Medicare's take-up of obesity care and the 2027–28 cash price rise. Plans that still cover require step therapy through Foundayo or oral semaglutide before tirzepatide or retatrutide. Pharmacy trend is still high single digits. Payers are lobbying for monthly products as an adherence fix.

pharma.state: Still a duopoly in the US, but Lilly widened its lead. The Indiana halt cost Novo an estimated 4–6 points of US share to Zepbound and Foundayo, and retatrutide gives Lilly the efficacy ceiling. Novo's response is CagriSema and the AUD programme. Ex-US prices keep eroding under generics. Amgen's MariTide filing is the first credible third US entrant.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on the drug is unremarkable, and being off it is what needs explaining. Among women 50–64 in the Phoenix–Scottsdale–Mesa suburbs, a weight-regain conversation now starts with 'Did you get hit by the shortage?' and only later reaches 'Did you stop?'. A visibly heavy middle-aged body in an insured circle is read as a coverage problem or a choice. A very thin older body is newly read as a fracture risk.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Medicare and Medicaid opt-in states made the drug ordinary for older and some poorer Americans at $50 or less. The cash-paying uninsured middle, aged 30–55, absorbed the 2027–28 price rise. The top third adds non-obese 'metabolic' use, so its thinness is now pharmacological maintenance, not only treatment. Border runs to Canadian pharmacies are a middle-class workaround in Michigan, Washington and Vermont.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are smaller and more scheduled. Hosts ask 'Are you dosing this week?' the way they once asked about allergies. Protein-forward menus dominate family gatherings with older relatives because of the bone guidance. Holiday 'drug holidays' are planned around Thanksgiving and weddings.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles in large metros commonly list 'on it' alongside 'sober-curious'; Hinge-style prompts about food noise are a meme. Couples negotiate dose schedules around anniversaries and trips. Reduced libido is a common complaint, and people raise it as the reason to take a planned holiday.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as a setting. The argument has moved from whether to medicate appetite to how much of the dial to turn, and how much enjoyment is acceptable to give up in exchange.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Fictional 2028 survey: ~27% of current users (≈12M adults) report flatness at some point, ~20% (≈9M) have taken dose reductions or 'holidays' to feel like themselves, and clinicians now ask about it routinely at dose escalation. It is reported more often at the high doses of tirzepatide and retatrutide. The 'quiet mind' telehealth market sells the same effect at low doses to people who want it.
interior_life.framing: Split three ways. Patients and the press call it a side effect ('the flats'). Telehealth wellness brands sell it as a feature ('quiet mind'). Addiction medicine treats it as therapy (alcohol use disorder). Many users simply describe it as a change in their character, with phrases like 'I'm a calmer person now' or 'I'm not funny anymore'.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Mixed and anecdotal, with some survey data. Users in finance, law and software commonly credit the drug with less distraction and fewer afternoon snack-and-scroll breaks. Salespeople and performers schedule dose holidays before high-stakes weeks. HR departments have no policy. A few employee assistance programmes added 'motivation changes on GLP-1' to their counselling menus.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Stand-up and sitcoms treat the flats as standard material. Musicians and writers argue publicly about whether working on the drug dulls their output, and several well-known novelists announced 'holiday drafts'. Intense-stimulus consumption grows: extreme-sour and extreme-spicy snacks, high-BPM workout playlists, escape rooms. Casual bar and casino attendance among heavy users keeps softening.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Reduced desire and emotional distance are among the most commonly cited reasons for drug holidays. Couples therapists report 'dose negotiation' as a recurring topic. Some partners describe the relationship as calmer and less volatile and prefer it that way.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable effect of reward blunting on political behaviour, and the claims made about it are partisan speculation. The drug itself became a 2028 campaign issue through the shortage and cash price rise, seniors' coverage, and the Canada price gap. Both parties claim the $245 Medicare price.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and pro-speed on approvals (CagriSema, retatrutide), alongside a sharper safety posture on bone and muscle (Drug Safety Communication, class label). Enforcement against compounders paused during the shortage-list window, then resumed with a wind-down.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Public subsidy widened: the CMS obesity model runs to 2031 at $245/$50, and 31 Medicaid states have opted in. Medicaid work requirements from 2027 cut eligibility for some bottom-third adults, partly offsetting the expansion.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Coverage is still conditioned on BMI/comorbidity criteria and prior authorisation. CMS guidance recommends functional screening at 12 months for enrollees 65+, but it is not a coverage condition. No adherence monitoring beyond refill data.
state.workforce_or_military: No change; no policy linking employment or service to use.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The Bloomington, Indiana fill-finish halt showed that US supply ran through a handful of domestic sites despite onshoring pledges. Personal importation from Canada is tolerated, while Health Canada limits dispensing to non-residents. The US-versus-India price gap (~$470 median US cash vs ~$6–40) is a routine campaign talking point.

events.event: CMS announces that the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot will become a multi-year Innovation Center model from Jan 2028 through 2031 at the same $245 payment and ~$50 copay, with loosened eligibility; 31 state Medicaid programmes opt in by mid-2028

FDA inspection findings halt filling at Novo Nordisk's Bloomington, Indiana site. Semaglutide injectables return to the FDA shortage list, which legally reopens 503A compounding. Novo raises cash Wegovy to $499 and rations new oral starts, Lilly ends low-tier Zepbound vial promotions, and the shortage is declared resolved in Jun 2028

Pooled Medicare and Danish registry analyses link rapid incretin weight loss in adults 65+ to a ~30% higher hip fracture risk. FDA issues a Drug Safety Communication, followed in Aug by class labelling on lean mass and bone density across all incretin obesity drugs
FDA approves Lilly's retatrutide (13 months after filing) at a $1,299 list price with dysesthesia and bone/lean-mass language; it is not yet included in the Medicare obesity model

National poll finds 17% of adults on an incretin drug and more than a quarter of users reporting 'the flats'. The same month, major telehealth brands roll out low-dose 'quiet mind' and longevity memberships aimed at people without obesity
events.driver: new_indications: mood_and_motivation, longevity_wellness; personality_layer: mainstream_complaint; cultural_response: normalisation

events.event: Amgen files a BLA for MariTide, the first monthly incretin injection, after phase 3 readouts; FDA decision expected no earlier than late 2029

open_tensions: Public programmes now pay ~$245 while cash and commercial payers absorbed the 2027–28 price shock. Taxpayers subsidise the old and poor at a fixed price while the uninsured middle pays nearly double, and the 2031 model end date arrives just as US exclusivity lapses.

The fracture signal falls hardest on the group that public coverage just made the default users (65+). Nobody has decided whether to cap weight loss in the old, require strength training, or simply label and watch.
Reward blunting is a complaint for ~a quarter of users and a product sold to people who want it. Monthly dosing (MariTide, filed) would remove the drug holidays people use to manage it.
~16M adults are off the drug after having been on it, and adolescents on it lack bone-accrual data. Six years of follow-up are beginning to show what long continuous use and cycling cost.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide in the US; brand exclusivity runs to roughly 2031–32 (access.generic_us false).
Medicare pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 beneficiary copay for covered obesity GLP-1s, the rate set in the Nov 2025 Lilly/Novo deals.
Wegovy list price remains $1,349/month, and almost nobody pays it.
Indian generic semaglutide remains available at single- to double-digit dollars per month, and Canada keeps its G7 generic approvals.
Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly remain the only companies selling branded incretin obesity drugs in the US; Foundayo's lowest dose is still $149 cash.

prose.headline: The Shortage Year: 45 Million Americans on a GLP-1, Their Pens on Backorder, Their Bones Under Watch
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2028, about one American adult in six takes an incretin drug, and in most suburbs nobody remarks on it. What people do remark on is someone who stopped. They ask whether it was the shortage, the price, or the doctor who mentioned bone density. Roughly sixteen million adults have been on the drug and are now off it. More than a third of everyone who has ever used it has stopped and started again at least once.

The federal government became the main payer almost by accident. The Medicare pilot that began in mid-2026 was supposed to be a bridge, but in January 2028 it became a multi-year model at the same $245 price and roughly $50 copay. Thirty-one state Medicaid programmes joined on the same terms. Public programmes now pay for about a third of all users and two in five new obesity starts, and they are effectively the default payer for anyone over 65. Employers noticed. Half of them have dropped weight-management coverage, and some say so directly: obesity care is Medicare's job now.

The cash market had a much harder year. In October 2027 FDA inspectors stopped filling lines at Novo Nordisk's Indiana plant. Semaglutide pens went back on the shortage list, and under the law that meant pharmacies could compound copies again, after two years of warning letters meant to stamp them out. The cash price of Wegovy rose from $349 to $499. Novo rationed its daily pill, which uses about seventy times as much active ingredient as the weekly shot. Lilly picked up the switchers, ended its cheapest vial offers, and gained share it is unlikely to give back. People in Detroit and Seattle drove to Canada for generics, and people elsewhere filled vials at compounding pharmacies. Some went without and regained about forty percent of their lost weight in eight months. Doctors now cite that interruption as the clearest real-world evidence that the drug works only while you take it. Medicare enrollees paid their fifty dollars throughout.

In March the bone data arrived. Medicare claims and Scandinavian registries agreed that older adults who lost weight fast on the drugs broke their hips about thirty percent more often. No single doctor would notice an increase that size, but across millions of patients it amounts to roughly six thousand extra hip fractures a year. The FDA updated every label in August. Geriatricians now talk about loss caps, and Medicare guidance recommends grip-strength tests and pays for strength-training referrals. Gyms have rebranded themselves as bone insurance, and CPG companies have added calcium to their protein bars. Lilly's retatrutide was approved in April with more than a quarter of body weight lost in trials, and it carries the new bone language on its label.

The drug is also widely understood to change how users feel. About a quarter of users describe 'the flats', a muted response to music, sex and jokes. Many manage it with planned breaks around weddings, launches and anniversaries. Stand-up comedians do whole sets about it. At the same time, telehealth companies sell low doses as 'quiet mind' memberships to people who have no obesity and want the stillness. Another five million affluent adults take the drug as a longevity habit. The effect people complain about in one group is being sold to another, and no regulator has said which description is right.

The food industry has adjusted rather than broken. Snack volumes are slightly lower, packs are smaller, and protein is on everything. Alcohol makers have had a harder time, because the heaviest drinkers, who buy most of the alcohol, are the people drinking less. Plus-size retailers keep closing stores.

In November Amgen filed for approval of a monthly injection. Payers see it as a fix for adherence, while some patients worry it would remove the breaks they use to manage the flats.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Alvarado wakes at six in Mesa and checks the pen in the butter compartment. It's Zepbound now. Last fall the pharmacy had no Wegovy for nine weeks, and her doctor switched her. Fifty dollars either way. Her neighbor Carol, sixty-one, pays four ninety-nine and complains about it at the mailbox.

At nine she drives to the clinic on Power Road. The technician has her squeeze a dynamometer, then stand up from a chair five times without her hands. 'Good,' he says, and writes something. The poster behind him shows a skeleton lifting a kettlebell.

At eleven it's resistance bands at the community center. Twelve women, two men, all gray. The instructor says 'bone loading' the way the priest says 'grace'. Denise's arms shake on the last set.

Lunch is cottage cheese and half a turkey sandwich. She saves the other half for tomorrow.

In the afternoon her daughter Marisol calls from Tucson about the quinceañera. 'I'm skipping my shot that week, Mom. I want to actually taste the cake. I want to dance like I mean it.' Denise doesn't answer right away. She has been thinking about skipping too. Not for the cake. She hasn't cried at a movie since March and isn't sure she minds.

At seven she watches a comedian on her phone. He's doing a bit about falling asleep during his own wedding toast. She smiles, which she thinks is the correct response.

At nine she sets out tomorrow's protein shake and takes her calcium. She tests the railing on the stairs before she goes up.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Half of them have dropped weight-management coverage, and some say so directly
least_plausible_claims.why: The world state says employer coverage fell from 60% to 50%, so about a sixth of covering employers dropped it, not half. The prose contradicts its own JSON, which is a mechanism and consistency failure.

least_plausible_claims.quote: or roughly 6,000 additional hip fractures a year across ~3.2M Medicare obesity-model users
least_plausible_claims.why: The HR of ~1.3 is stated only for 65+ users with rapid ≥15% loss, but it is applied to all 3.2M model users, who are not all 65+ or rapid losers. The headline excess is overstated, which is a reconciliation gap.

1.1% of under-18s is roughly 800k youths, or over 3% of all 12–17s. That is a large jump from a 2026 baseline where child use was rare and about 0.6% of children with obesity, and no event or driver supplies a mechanism.

rationale.badness: The world is a recognisably harder society, not a collapsed one. Harms are an older-adult fracture signal (~6,000 excess hip fractures a year), a cash-paying middle squeezed by the shortage, and 27% of users reporting 'the flats'. There is no data on adolescent bone accrual and about 16M people are cycling off. Inequality shows in the public/cash split and the Canada border runs. Epistemic harm is moderate because the harms are named, surveyed and labelled, though the feature/bug ambiguity of 'quiet mind' remains unresolved.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: All ten drivers are traceable: 17% on-drug, the cash price shock, Medicare and Medicaid expansion, bone and muscle labelling, the MariTide filing as the allowed form of the monthly launch, and mainstream flatness. A supply halt and shortage listing sit uneasily beside market_shock 'none', and FDA actions sit beside state_action 'none'. mechanism: The shortage chain (Bloomington halt, shortage listing, 503A reopening, price rise) is shown well. Weaker points are the prose saying 'Half of them have dropped' coverage against JSON 60→50, and the pediatric 1.1% and the 27% flatness figure arriving with little causal chain. magnitude: Population figures (17/23), the income and age bands (check ≈17.2), approvals (CagriSema, retatrutide at 13 months, survodutide, MariTide filing) and the spending arithmetic ($9.4B, $6.5B, $4.2B, 15M/45M payer mix) all sit inside the envelope and reconcile. Minor flaws are the fracture-count extrapolation and the large pediatric share.
rationale.generativity: The Denise Alvarado day carries strong texture: the dynamometer, the poster of a skeleton lifting a kettlebell, 'bone loading' said like 'grace', her daughter skipping a shot for a quinceañera, and not crying at a movie. The world fields add the Phoenix regain conversation, 'Are you dosing this week?', holiday drafts by novelists and planned drug holidays. Many implied characters and scenes follow.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Baseline hip fracture risk is ~0.7%/yr in this group, so the excess is ~0.2 pp/yr, or roughly 6,000 additional hip fractures a year across ~3.2M Medicare obesity-model users.
least_plausible_claims.why: magnitude/mechanism: The 1.3 hazard ratio applies only to users with rapid ≥15% loss, yet the excess is applied to all 3.2M model users. The Medicare obesity model only began Jul 2026, so few enrollees could have had two years of exposure by the Mar 2028 analysis.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Half of them have dropped weight-management coverage
least_plausible_claims.why: mechanism: The world state says employer coverage fell from 60% to 50%, which is about a sixth of covering employers dropping it, not half. The prose contradicts the JSON.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Novo rationed new oral Wegovy starts, because the 25 mg daily oral uses roughly 70× the API of a weekly 2.4 mg injection.
least_plausible_claims.why: mechanism: The stated trigger is a fill-finish halt for injectables, which does not constrain oral API supply. Rationing the oral is asserted with an API-scarcity rationale that the candidate never shows.
